staged_description.title: Flag Burning Criminalization - Defying Supreme Court Rulings
staged_description.description_short: Flag Burning Criminalization - Defying Supreme Court Rulings
staged_description.description_medium: In August 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing federal prosecutors to pursue cases related to flag burning and threatening jail time for people who burned the U.S. flag. The order challenged the Supreme Court’s 1989 ruling in Texas v. Johnson, which treats flag burning as protected symbolic speech. The directive did not itself overturn that precedent or make protected expression a valid crime.
staged_description.description_long: Donald Trump signed an executive order attempting to criminalize flag burning and impose one-year jail sentences for the constitutionally protected form of political protest, openly defying the Supreme Court's 1989 ruling in Texas v. Johnson that established flag burning as symbolic speech protected under the First Amendment. Trump declared 'If you burn a flag, you get one year in jail, no early exits, no nothing. And it goes on your record and you'll see flag burning stop immediately' while directing Attorney General Pam Bondi to 'vigorously prosecute' flag burners. The order represented an unprecedented presidential attempt to criminalize constitutionally protected expression through executive decree, with Trump claiming without evidence that 'foreign nationals are using flag burning to intimidate and threaten American citizens.' The Foundation for Individual Rights in Education warned that 'Trump may think he has the power to override the First Amendment with the stroke of a pen, but he doesn't,' emphasizing that 'the government can't criminalize protected expressive activity.' The executive order attempted to sidestep the Supreme Court precedent by directing prosecution for 'related crimes' during flag burning incidents, while threatening visa revocation and deportation for foreign nationals who engage in the protected political expression. Free speech organizations called the order a dangerous precedent that could lead to criminalizing other forms of political protest, with Trump's defiance of established constitutional law representing an authoritarian rejection of judicial authority over executive power.

The analysis also says Project 2025 proposes eliminating existing DOJ consent decrees; at the time, nearly 30 agreements covered law-enforcement and jail systems. These are proposals and the Center’s assessment of their likely effects, not evidence that every provision became policy. The analysis supports a description of possible federal intervention in local prosecutorial decisions and changes to oversight agreements. staged_description.description_short: Supreme Court Lets Prosecutors Seek Trump Tax Returns After Years of Stonewalling
staged_description.description_medium: After years of fighting subpoenas, the Supreme Court ruled that prosecutors could seek Trump's financial records, including tax returns, and that Congress could pursue them under limits. staged_description.description_long:
On July 9, 2020, the Supreme Court ruled in two cases involving subpoenas for Donald Trump’s financial records. In Trump v. Vance, it rejected the claim that a sitting president had absolute immunity from a state grand-jury subpoena, while allowing Trump to raise ordinary objections. In Trump v. Mazars, the Court sent congressional subpoenas back for further review under a more demanding standard. The decisions allowed legal processes to continue but did not order immediate public release of the tax returns.

The rulings were a setback to Trump’s broad immunity arguments after years of litigation over access to his financial information. They did not decide whether the records would ultimately be disclosed or whether the subpoenas were valid in every respect. The distinction between prosecutor access and congressional access is important: each case involved a different requester and legal test. The event concerns the Court’s limits on presidential immunity and its instructions for further review, not a final judgment on the contents of Trump’s finances.

staged_description.description_long: Haley and Pompeo announced the U.S. withdrawal from the U.N. Human Rights Council at the State Department on June 19, 2018. The council is a United Nations body that reviews the human-rights records of member states and adopts resolutions and recommendations. Haley criticized what she described as persistent bias against Israel and objected to the council’s membership of governments accused of serious abuses. She said the United States had sought reforms but would not remain a member if the body continued to operate as she described. Critics, including human-rights organizations and U.N. officials, argued that leaving surrendered a seat and reduced U.S. influence over investigations and debate. The withdrawal did not dissolve the council or prevent the United States from engaging with it as an observer, but it ended U.S. membership during the remainder of the term. President Biden’s administration announced a return in 2021 and later secured election to a new term. The episode was thus a withdrawal from a multilateral oversight forum followed by a later policy reversal. It should be distinguished from the separate question of whether the council’s performance warranted reform.

staged_description.description_medium: In April 2026, Democrats in the House and Senate introduced resolutions to overturn a Trump administration rule changing eligibility for Public Service Loan Forgiveness. The rule lets the Education Department remove borrowers whose employers are deemed to have a “substantial illegal purpose,” and was scheduled to take effect in July. Democrats said it could target organizations serving immigrants and transgender youth; the measure was unlikely to pass.
staged_description.description_long: The Public Service Loan Forgiveness program cancels federal student loans for eligible borrowers after 10 years of payments while working for qualifying public-service employers, including government agencies, public schools, fire and police departments, public hospitals and nonprofits. In fall 2025, the Trump administration issued a rule allowing the Education Department to remove borrowers from the program if their employer was found to have a “substantial illegal purpose.” The rule was scheduled to take effect in July 2026 and was aimed primarily at organizations working with immigrants and transgender youth, according to the Associated Press. On April 14, Democrats in both the House and Senate introduced resolutions seeking to overturn the change. They argued that the rule was political and could deprive some borrowers of relief they had been promised, while describing it as an attempt to intimidate or punish certain organizations. The resolutions could receive a vote, but AP reported they were unlikely to pass. The dispute concerned whether an employer’s activities could disqualify its workers from a loan-forgiveness program, not an immediate cancellation of the program itself. At the time of the report, the rule had not yet taken effect. Its implementation and the effort to reverse it therefore remained unresolved, leaving affected borrowers and employers awaiting the July start date and any congressional action.

staged_description.description_short: Trump: Tony Schwartz publishes negative Trump story, Trump hires him
staged_description.description_medium: In 1985, Tony Schwartz published a critical New York magazine profile of Donald Trump, who nevertheless praised the piece and sent Schwartz a fan note. Later that year, Trump offered Schwartz half the advance and royalties to ghostwrite The Art of the Deal. Schwartz accepted, and the book project began a close working relationship that lasted eighteen months.
staged_description.description_long: Tony Schwartz’s 1985 New York magazine story presented Donald Trump as a struggling landlord rather than the triumphant developer celebrated in his public image. Schwartz described Trump’s unsuccessful effort to remove rent-controlled tenants from a building on Central Park South, including a plan to place homeless people in the building to pressure residents. The magazine’s cover showed Trump sweaty and unshaven. The New Yorker later reported that Trump liked the critical story, displayed its cover in his office and sent Schwartz a complimentary note. The two met again when Schwartz interviewed Trump for Playboy. Trump said he had signed a book deal and needed to save material for the project; Schwartz suggested the title The Art of the Deal. After considering the offer for several weeks, Schwartz agreed to ghostwrite the book in exchange for half the advance and half the royalties. Trump accepted those terms. Beginning in late 1985, Schwartz spent eighteen months working closely with Trump, including time at his office, meetings and homes. The resulting 1987 book carried both men’s names and became a bestseller. The episode connects a critical profile to the later collaboration that helped shape Trump’s public image.
